maintopic: NATIONAL BATTLEFIELDS COMMISSION-PURCHASE OF LANDS AT QUEBEC.

speechtext:
Sir WILFRID LAURIER (Prime Minister) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 219) respecting the National Battlefields at Quebec. He said :	This Bill is introduced in consequence of the resolution adopted by the National Battlefields Commission which has been communicated to me as follows :
At a meeting of the National Battlefields Commission, held on the 16th instant, the following resolution was adopted:
Resolved, whereas the great work entailed in the .tercentenary celebration of the founding of Quebec has absorbed all the time of the National Battlefields Commission; whereas it is most expedient that the commission should be empowered to secure without undue delay certain properties belonging to private parties and which will be required for the Battlefield park j whereas section 10 of the Aot constituting the commission requires the authority of parliament before any land or immovable property is purchased or acquired by the commission; whereas delay means the enhancing in value of many of the said properties which might at present be obtained at a much lower figure than would be likely later; the National Battlefields Commission urgently recommends that the Act respecting the National Battlefields at Quebec be amended so as to empower the commission, subject to the previous authority of the Governor in Council, to acquire if necessary, any or all of the properties specified in a memorandum sent to the Governor General in Council on the fifteenth day of July instant such properties as are not mentioned in the said memorandum to remain subject to clause 10 of the said Act.

Chairman, National Battlefields Commission.
Section 10, which is here referred to, reads as follows :
No land or immovable property shall be purchased or acquired by the commission except with the previous authority of parliament.
This law relates not merely to the money voted by parliament bnt to ail other moneys which come into the hands of the commission ; none of these moneys may be used for tlie purchase of lands except with the previous authority of parliament. As the imblic know?, large sums have been subscribed to the Battlefields Commission, and it is expeceted that the Prince of Wales will hand over the money to the commission with some statement made to him of the property which it is intended immediately to acquire for the purpose of creating a Battlefields park. I have a plan, here which * Mr. FIELDING.
I will place in the hands of hon. gentlemen on the other side, showing the property which it is intended to acquire. This property is described in the following statement prepared by Mr. E. G. Meredith, notary public .

The only objection which I can see ter this Bill at the present time is that no maximum purchase price is fixed. I pointed. that out In Quebec, and I asked if it were not possible to fix a maximum price, and I received this telegram from His Excellency :
Description of property battlefields mailed yesterday, terms of sales not yet arranged as owners of scheduled property advancing price daily. Think commission should be empowered to use moneys already subscribed for purchase.
The Bill, therefore, which I introduced is as follows :
An Act Respecting the National Battlefields at Quebec.
Whereas the National Battlefields Commission has requested that it he empowered to purchase, acquire and hold the lands or immovable property hereinafter referred to, and'it is expedient to comply with such request: therefore His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows :-[DOT]
1. The National Battlefields Commission may subject to the approval of the Governor in Council, purchase, acquire and hold the lands and immovable property set forth and described in the schedule to this Act.
Then follows the schedule which I have read.

When the Act now
proposed to be amended came before parliament this session, objection was taken by several hon. gentlemen to the provisions of section 5 which read :
The commission may purchase, acquire and hold the lands or immovable property in the city of Quebec, or in the vicinity thereof, where the great battles were fought, or which were occupied by the various commands of the respective armies upon the battlefields.
The section is very indefinite as to the extent of lands proposed to be purchased, and it seems to confer upon the commission a very wide power which might commit the people of this country to an enormous expenditure, the extent of which cannot be foretold. There was very little information before the House at the time and by reason of the paucity of information clause 10 to which the Prime Minister has just called attention was inserted, and It reads :

No lands or immovable property shall be purchased or acquired by the commission except with the previous authority of parliament, and no expenditure shall be made by the commission until it has been approved by parliament.
It is beyond question that the measure as introduced would have involved a very protracted debate and would have encountered very strong opposition if it had not been for the insertion of a provision of that kind. I think it was I who suggested that provision, but I did not suggest it exactly in that form. The amendment which the Prime Minister inserted in the Bill in accordance with my suggestion went beyond the scope of what I proposed. What I recollect to have proposed on that occasion was that no moneys voted by this parliament should be expended for any such purpose unless with the previous approval of parliament. This parliament voted the sum of $300,000 by section 8 of the Act to be paid over to the commission, and by section 10 it was provided that the whole or a portion of that amount might be devoted to the purposes of the celebration which is to take place during the coming week. But apart from the moneys which were to be derived by the commission from the parliament of Canada there were other moneys, the anticipated origin of which is set forth in section 7. The commission was authorized to receive moneys contributed not only by this parliament but by the different legislatures of the provinces, or by any municipal or other body, or by any private individual for the purposes of the Act. So far as the money voted by this parliament is concerned it might be and no doubt was a very proper thing to insert the provision which is embodied in section 10, but In as much as a very large amount of the moneys now available to the commission have been derived, not from the vote of this parliament but from other sources, I am inclined to think parliament might intrust to the Governor in Council the supervision of the expenditure of these moneys for the purposes mentioned in the Act, now proposed by the Prime Minister. Possibly a word or two in amendment of the Act, as just, now introduced, might be inserted. So far as I am personally concerned I would not insist very much on that.- It may be said of course that information should be given to parliament with regard to the price proposed to be paid, and I would think that the commission would do well n it to be in too great haste if such haste should involve the payment of any exorbitant sum for any portion of this land. It will be remembered by hon. gentlemen that section G of the statute confers upon the commission all the powers of expropriation with which any railway company is invested under the Railway Act for the purposes of its undertaking. In that provision the commission has a very effective safeguard against the payment of any exorbit-

ant price, and bearing that in mind and also that the proposed purchase is to be subject to the approval and supervision of the Governor in Council, for my part I do not see any objection to the legislation which the Prime Minister proposes.

It seems to me that under the legislation which was passed with regard to these national battlefields, the commission entered upon a campaign of money collection, and that there was an agreement or contract entered into between the subscribers to that fund and the commission or this parliament, that the conditions under which the commission was appointed and the duties prescribed for them and the power given them, were to be maintained. It was under these conditions the subscriptions were made. Now these conditions are proposed to be removed, and proposed to be removed at this, the last day of the session when there is no time to consider these matters. But there is a plea of urgency. Urgency is a plea that has been made to do service on many occasions. Where can possibly be the urgency ? The people who own these lands on the Plains of Abraham have known for many months that there was a proposition to acquire them for a national park, and why has it become so suddenly urgent that these lands should be acquired by the commission ? What has caused the price to go up so rapidly just at this juncture? I cannot see anything in that plea at all. I do not see any sufficient reason put forward wThy the tacit contract or agreement between this parliament and the gentlemen and legislatures who have subscribed to this fund, should be violated. Let this national commission take options upon this property. Parliament will meet soon again, a new parliament, it is true, but parliament will meet in the course of a very few months before the new year. Let the commission take four or five months option upon this property, and then parliament will be in a position to deal with it.
I do not see any necessity for this Bill, and I must protest against it.
Is it correct to say that the grant that has been made by parliament of $300,000 is none of it available for the purchase of this land ? Has all that land been taken by the commission ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The greater part of the land has already been appropriated by the commission, and I am told the whole of it will be subscribed.
Not for the purchase of land ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Not for the purchase of land. If my hon. friend will refer to the discussion which took place in this House at the time of the second reading of the Bill he will see that there was a vigorous insistence that all moneys, both

moneys voted by parliament and moneys coming from other sources, should be subject to the control of parliament. This was particularly in view of the possible purchase of the Ross rifle factory. The Ross rifle factory is not included in the present grant of land.
I understood the Prime Minister to say that none of the Ross rifle property is included.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is correct.
Without attempting to debate this question, I merely wish to enter my protest against the passage of this Bill at this late hour of the session.
As one that voted against this enormous grant, I must enter my protest against this proposition in the last hours of the session. I think we might well afford to wait until parliament meets again.

As I understand the matter, when we did put this saving clause in the last Act, section 10, I think, people would understand that before we disposed of the money we would thoroughly investigate the circumstances. I think that duty is cast upon us, and I regret that at this time of the session the right hon. gentleman lias brought this matter up. I do not blame the administration for not having brought it up sooner, because I presume they could not bring it up until about this time. In the meantime, I think we are not right in disposing of this money that the people have contributed, without knowing more of the circumstances than we do. The Prime Minister says that we are not by this attempting to purchase the Ross rifle property. That is true, but we are committing ourselves to a scheme which will involve in the end the purchase of that factory. Whilst I realize that we have uo time to discuss the matter now, if I had control of the situation I would not sanction the proposal of this money at the present time. So far as I am concerned. I throw upon the government the entire onus of seeing that what is right is done in this matter.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the first and second time and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,

I think the Prime Minister should explain where the urgency for this Bill exists. It may be necessary to do, it at some time, but I do not see any present necessity. Why won't it do just as well four or five months from now ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have stated that the only authority we have is a resolution of the Battlefields Commission, which pleads urgency for this measure.

The right hon. gentleman did not give any reasons, even today, to show necessity. Why cannot a better bargain be made in the fall of the year or next spring when parliament will be in session? Generally speaking, in a hasty bargain the country gets the worst of it and the other fellow gets the best of it. Although I understand the commission as saying that it is necessary, I take that to mean that it is going to be in the near future. But surely it is not absolutely vital that it shall be done next week? The land is not going to run away, the affairs of the country will still be going on and I do. not see any reason for doing it now without the information which we ought to have. It is a matter which might be thoroughly investigated, and unless there is some great urgency I am bound to say that I must protest against the Bill passing.

There does not seem to. be any reason why we should accept the ipse dixit of the commission or that this parliament cannot perform its duties without a direction from the commission. We must hold ourselves responsible for the way the money is used, for the trust which is given to us by those who subscribed this money.
As I understand it, this Act is absolutely independent of and makes no change in the National Battlefields Act as we passed it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: With this exception only nothing is changed.
It makes no change in any other particular ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.
This is an Act which stands entirely by itself for this one purpose and no other?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is right.
The Governor in Council is authorized to approve of the purchase and holding of this land and no other?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No other.

Then the Bill remains to apply to all other purchases that are made and none of these purchases can be consummated without coming to parliament and asking the assent of parliament thereto? What is the extent of the land that is being purchased ? There are rings and edges around the other part of the land. I could not tell from that plan which the right hon. gentleman has shown us what already belongs to the government. I take it as a matter of fact that the waste land of the government will become part of the National Battlefields. I cannot tell anything from that plan as to whether, when this purchase is made to go with what the government owns and which is not occupied by the rifle factory, we will have any more

than eight or ten lumps of land scattered here and there, or whether it is to help to fill out or complete a portion of land which lies altogether and becomes a connected part. If we are just to have patches of land here and there throughout the city and call that a park it does not amount to much.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If I had the plan I could show my hon. friend what we propose to purchase.

I would like to say that there is a feeling abroad that there will be a great deal of extravagance in connection with this undertaking. Now, when the government is proposing to make changes, giving wider and greater power to the commission it is important that the government should point out that this is likely to run into an enormous expenditure. For myself I think it would be better if the government would halt a little until parliament sees how these men will expend the money and the amount of caution they will exercise in the expenditure of it before they are given wider powers. I do not wish to enter any very strong protest, but I do say that it is unfortunate that the government, at this very late hour, should introduce this legislation, and I hope the government will direct the attention of these gentlemen to the fact that they have great powers and that they must exercise great caution or they may call upon parliament to appropriate a larger amount than the people are willing to pay.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think it will be doing my hon. friend (Mr. Blain) no injustice to say I do not believe he has any undue confidence in this government; I cannot understand him suggesting that we should make a recommendation to a commission, which, in his opinion, ought to be composed of far better men than we are. One member of the commission is Mr. Gar-neau. Perhaps my hon. friend does not know Mr. Garneau. He is the mayor of Quebec. The next commissioner is Senator Sir George Drummond, in whom my hon. friend must have confidence. The next member of the commission is Colonel Denison, and I think my hon. friend must also have confidence in Colonel Denison.
Mr. FOSTER, He will keep order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The fourth commissioner is Mr. Walker, of the Bank of Commerce.
He will hold the purse strings.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think he can be trusted. The next commissioner is Mr. Turgeon, and if Mr. Turgeon is inclined to be, as we are supposed to be, extravagant, he will be checked by the other members of the commission; so that I
think my hon. friend's opinions are utterly uncalled for.
While we may have the utmost confidence in these men, I must say that recently they have got into very bad company.

When we began about this national battlefield the idea seemed to be generally approved of, and we thought that this commission would be able to look over the whole matter, arrive at its plans, and submit to parliament a proposal as to what it intended to do, so that we would know just exactly what was meant by the National Battlefields park. We thought we would know how much ground we were going to have and how it was proposed to lay it out and beautify it, and that an estimate of the whole cost would be given. What I object to, and I think it is a valid objection, is that you buy a little piece here and a little piece there and a little in another place, and there is absolutely no general plan at all as to what we are going to have. No general information is given to ns as to what the scheme will be when it is all thought out. I would like to have seen the commissioners propose their plan, and then let that plan be submitted for the information of the House. As I understand it, the whole of the Seminary property is to be bought by them. I cannot see why it is necessary to buy the whole block of Seminary land. What the commissioners seem to be aiming at is to get certain broad driveways that will be good for a park, but broad driveways will also be good for the city of Quebec and the locality. What you are really doing is constituting a system of broadened avenues for the city of Quebec, just as your Improvement Commission in Ottawa has splendid driveways here. Whether it be a necessary part of the National Battlefields plan to improve the driveways of the city of Quebec is a question, unless we knew that the park itself was adjacent to these driveways, and it does not appear that it is. The plan which the Prime Minister has given us to-day does not delimit the ground that we will own, but, as it looks from that plan, here is a block owned by us there, there is a portion that we do not own and there is another little piece that we do own, and so it is cut up in that way. It seems to be the purpose of the commission to have a broad driveway connecting the Plains of Abraham proper with other portions of the city. Is it necessary, in order to have that driveway, to buy the whole of that Seminary land, or cannot a right of way for the driveway lie secured through it? I understand it is the purpose to divide that property up into lots and sell it. As a matter of real finance the Seminary could very well afford to say fo the Battlefields Commission :

Give ns a good driveway through that property, embellish and adorn it, It will make our property many times more valuable than it is ; we are going to sell it for town lots anyway, and we will give you the right of way. Now, you propose to buy the whole of it. and it will cost a great deal of money. Why do we need the whole of it? Why cannot an arrangement be made to have a driveway through it, which would largely appreciate the property, without putting the Battlefields Commission to the cost of the whole of it? Those are the thoughts that occurred to me.

I was not in the House when this matter was first discussed. Does it apply only to the battlefields on the Plains of Abraham, or is it the intention to purchase every battlefield throughout the country and make parks?
Why don't the British buy the field of Waterloo ?	,

At the outset I was in favour of having the commission take over the whole Plains of Abraham, even to a greater extent than is proposed in the present amendment to the Bill. From my viewpoint I do not think it would be becoming to see any private property remaining in the middle of the Plains of Abraham. In my opinion, it would be well to take the whole bank of the river along where the vai'ious stages of the battle of the Plains of Abraham were fought, so that there might be one uninterrupted stretch of land from the citadel clear away to the right hand side of the plains. The visitor to Quebec Ito-day will find only a little 10-acre field available for the great review of troops at the Tercentenary. If the plan were carried out as I have outlined, and if the Ross Rifle Company were given a site for their factory elsewhere, and if the government moved the building from the Plains of Abraham, then with the present amendment the thing would be pretty nearly complete. That jail on the Plains of Abraham is an eyesore ; it is right on the spot where the French forces stood during the engagement. Wolfe's monument is better surrounded now than it was before, but it is within a hundred feet of back yards. To my mind, the best plan would be to make a clean sweep from the citadel off to the right and up to where the grand stand is now being erected for the pageant. That would necessitate the purchase of certain property, but it is not so large as it looks on the map. The Ross rifle' factory bugaboo could be overcome by the minister selecting a site somewhere else and moving the whole factory there. I do not think it would be a very expensive job if it were gone about in a business way to get that whole land clean from the citadel away up to the right, and then, in case of a great
review of troops, -there would be plenty of room to manoeuvre. Even from the point of view of defence it would be well to have that part of the plains free from buildings.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In answer to the question of my hon. friend from Kings (Mr. Fowler), I may say that section 5 creates the commission and states its objects to be :
The commission may purchase, acquire and hold the lands or immovable property in the city of Quebec, or in the vicinity thereof, where the great battles were fought, or which were occupied by the various commands of the respective armies upon the battlefields.
It does not go beyond the city of Quebec and the vicinity; it is connected simply with the events of 1759 and 1760. In reply to my hon. friend from Toronto I might say that it would have been a good idea had the commission submitted a report of what they intend to do, but the correspondence which I have had shows that the property is rising rapidly in price every day and the longer the purchase is delayed the greater the cost will be. With regard to the property of the Seminary, I may say that the Seminary own a pretty large piece of land there. They have cut it up into town lots. The commission have decided, and very properly in my judgment, to acquire this property. The object of the commission is to make a park which will include all the land where the battle took place, and the visitor to Quebec will be enabled to see the very spot where Wolfe landed and brought up his troops. The second battlefield of 1760 will also be converted into a park.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
Mr. FIELDING moved that item 64 in Public Bills and Orders-second reading of Bill (No. 187) from the Senate, to amend the Canada Temperance Act.-Mr. Black- be now called.

I have no objection to this item being called, but 1 call attention to the fact that it has been on the Order-Paper since June 17, and one would have supposed that, if the government desired to have the Bill passed, they would not have postponed its consideration until the very last day of the session. Why is it that the consideration of so important a Bill has been left so long ?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have reached the stage of the session when, in the general cleaning up, we are taking up matters of general importance which are not on the Order Paper. That is the only reason.
So far as the order is concerned, my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) has taken up the last Bill in the list of public Bills and Orders, instead of beginning at the beginning.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not proposing to follow the order in which the Bills appear on the Order Paper. We have some regard for their order in importance.
Motion agreed and Order called.
Bill read the second time.
The Bill stands in the name of the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Black) but I understood that the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) would take charge of the Bill.

I would direct the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) to the fact that this is a piece of temperance legislation, and would ask him whether it will embody a clause for the abolition of the bar in the House of Commons.	-
Has not that been abolished long ago ?
It was in full blast yesterday.

PICKUP This Bill is for the purpose of amending the Canada Temperance Act. Twelve counties out of the eighteen in Nova Scotia have adopted the Canada Temperance Act, known as the Scott Act, Two counties, for reasons peculiar to those districts, have voted to have the Act repealed so that at present ten counties in the province are under the operation of the Act. The Act has proven very efficient where the sentiments of the people' are in favour of its enforcement. The principal amendment sought by this Bill is to prohibit the carriage of liquor from a license county to a Scott Act county. This legislation only applies to districts where the people by their votes ask that no liquor be sold, and does not apply to any province or district that has not adopted the Act. It is only fair that the wishes of the people be met There are three amendments covered by this Bill, and all are necessary to satisfactorily carry out the Act.
House went into committee on the Bill.
On section 1,

As this is an extension of the -Canada Temperance Act, I would ask the hon. member who is in charge of the Bill whether or not, in order to continue this Act in operation in these counties, it will be necessary again to submit it to the electors? I understand that this Canada Temperance Act comes into operation only on approval of the peo pie. Now, if we materially alter it and incorporate in it much larger powei-s, would Mr. FIELDING.
the effect be that the people would have to vote upon it again, and express approval of the new conditions, in order to continue its operations ? We should be very careful that we do not destroy the Act iu attempts to amend it.
Mi-. FOWLER. There is a decision on that point. It does not need to be voted on again.

Yes.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Reference was made last night by the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) to item No. 63, Bill (No. 178) from the Senate, relating to the water carriage of goods. If there be no objection and any hon. member interested in the Bill will move the second reading, I should be glad to move that the order be called.
The hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) does not come very often ; I do not see why he should have special privileges and I would object.

I think this Bill relates to too important a matter to be taken up at this time when there is no proper opportunity for due consideration of the Bill. I find there are some very drastic changes proposed and I do not think we should be called upon to legislate in regard to this matter at this time.

I protest in exactly the same way. I do not know what the Bill is, it has never been before this House, it may be a most important Bill and a very salutary Bill but it is not right to ask us, two or three hours before the House prorogues with scarcely more than a quorum present, to undertake its consideration.

It is a matter of very great regret that the government did not take this up before. It has been on the order paper since May 29, it would have occupied only five minutes to give the Bill its first reading and send it to a special committee where it could have been investigated and progress could have been made without delaying the House for more than a few minutes. Instead of that no action has been taken by the government respecting a subject of great importance not only to the shipping interests but more especially to the shippers and producers and similar other interests as well. The Bill has rested untouched on the order paper since May 29, and now it is proposed, at nearly 1 o'clock on Saturday, the last working day of the session we hope, to have that Bill considered. Such a proposal is really grotesque in its absurdity. Why was the Bill

not sent long ago to a subcommittee of this House for the purpose of making an investigation similar to that which has been made in the Senate ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This Bill, although an Important one, possibly, was never a government Bill, it was brought in by a private member of the Senate and sent here in the ordinary course of business. In cleaning up the business of the session, attention was called to it and I mentioned it to the House. It is not a government Bill and it was not the duty of the government to send it to a committee. I brought it up at the request of the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean).

The Bill stands in my name but I am not the promoter. The promoter of the Bill, Senator Campbell, has had several discussions with me within the last few days. He expressed considerable anxiety as to its fate. He represents that very large interests particularly in Ontario desired that this Bill should be pressed to an issue at this session. He represents it as very important, personally I know very little about it. When the Bill was introduced in the Senate objection was taken to it by the shipping interests in Montreal and elsewhere and representatives of those interests appeared before the committee of the Senate. Senator Campbell represented to me that the representative of the shipping interest has consented to the Bill and directed my attention to the observations of Mr. Meredith who appeared before the committee of the Senate. The members have the report of Mr. Meredith's statement and I need not detain them.
The people are pressing for it.

The fact that there was a controversy over it in the Senate indicates that the question is so vast, that the changes made by the Bill are so radical, that we should have at least a special committee of this House to take evidence with regard to this matter and report to the House. There is no ground for making an exception in the case of this Bill. The Minister of Railways ten days ago refused to deal with a level crossings Bill which this House passed unanimously, and when it was amended by the Senate and sent back here, the Minister of Railways refused to deal with it because it was too late in the session, and that was ten days ago. Although my Bill was dealing with a very grave matter involving the lives of men, women and children at railway crossings, the Minister of Railways refused to make an exception in its favour. If an exception could not apply to a Bill of that importance, then it ought not to apply to this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is evident from the difference of opinion concerning this Bill that it cannot go through. I move therefor for leave to withdraw the motion.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext:
I received the following message from the Canadian Manufacturers' Association :
Toronto, July 16, 1906.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier,
House of Commons, Ottawa. ^
The executive council of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association now in session, knowing that under existing tariff conditions a number of our largest Canadian woollen industries must suffer annihilation before another year, appeal to you for immediate relief. What two hundred woollen manufacturers have asked of you in the memorandum submitted is the least that will save them from ruin. They, together with the thousands of working people dependent upon them for their daily bread, and the farmers who have hitherto found profitable employment in wool growing, join us in the firm stand that this important question must be disposed of before the closing of parliament. The association awaits your answer.
(Sgd.) Canadian Manufacturers' Association.
I replied on the same day as follows :
Telegram.
Ottawa, July 16, 1908. Canadian Manufacturers' Association,
Toronto, Ont.
Government regret that with present information they are unable to agree to the proposals respecting increased duties on wool goods. In a country with the climate of Canada the cost of woollen clothing te:omes a question of very great importance. A proposal to increase the taxes on what might almost be called a necessary^ of life naturally arouses much opposition among the consumers and their representatives. The government have on more than one occasion given evidence of their appreciation of the importance, of the woollen interests and their desire to give reasonable encouragement to it. They hope that to some extent the difficulties which the manufacturers are meeting are due not to tariff conditions but to a depression in trade which they believe is but temporary. This view is supported by the fact that in the neighbouring republic where a very high wool tariff is in operation there has been trade depression. The government, with due regard to the people of all 'sections of the country, feel that this is not the moment at which they should adopt a policy of increased taxation, especially on articles of a necessary character. The complaints that have been made by the woollen trade as to evasions of the Customs laws are being carefully looked into and if it be ascertained tbat they he well founded, the proper remedy will be applied. The questions of tariff revision as respects the woollen industries cannot possibly be dealt with in the few hours of this session that remain. We can assure the manufacturers' that we are fully appeciative of the industry and that if we cannot at thi9 stage meet their wishes it is because we are obliged to consider the wishes of all classes throughout the country.
(Sgd.) WILFRID LAURIER.

Consideration of amendments made by the Senate to Bill (No. 1S9) to amend the Civil Service Act.-Mr. Fisher.
I would like to have some explanation of these amendments.

The only change of importance is the addition of a section bringing the Act into force on the 1st September. The other amendments are simply verbal alterations tbat, in the opinion of the Senate make the Act clearer, but do not change the meaning.

I would not be inclined to agree with the view of the Minister of Agriculture with respect to the Senate amendment to section 45. I observe that at the end of the section the Senate has added the following words :
Or if such action is required during the recess of parliament, by the Governor m Council, subject to ratification by the two Houses at the next ensuing session.
I do not appreciate the necessity of that amendment.

This amendment has been urged by the chief officers of the two Houses and especially by the librarians of parliament. During the recess there is absolutely no authority in the Act to enable anything to be done.
Enable what to be done? 1 have not a copy of these amendments.

I would be glad to go over the amendments seriatim. The first amendment is one to paragraph 2 and is in the following words :
The word ' now ' when used in this Act shall mean the date of its coming into force.
That is necessary by reason of the fact that the Act will come into force on the 1st September. The next amendment is to clause 8. Clause 8 reads as follows :
As soon as practicable after the conning into force of the Act. the head of each department shall oause the organization of his department to be determined and defined by order in council.
The Senate have added the following words :
Due regard being lnad to the present status of each officer or clerk, as the case may be.
BORDEN What do they mean by that ?
I understand that they mean simply to safeguard the present position of the clerks. I did not think it necessary but the Senate wished these words in.

If they have an effect at all they prevent the object that the clause seems to call for. By saying ' due regard being had to the present status of each officer or clerk as the ease may be ' the minister's action is restricted ; how can he reorganize his department ?

I do not think the words have the effect my hon. friend fears. I thought the clause without them meant that and I did not consider these words altered the sense of the clause. The next amendment is in clause 38 which would now read :
Notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act or any words to the like effect shall be deemed sufficient to authorize the payment of any such salary or remuneration.
1 think that makes it clearer.
The next amendment is in clause 45 in the 25th line where they have inserted ' or under the Civil Service Act.' speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the items for the Customs Department were concurred in some time ago, I shall not have an opportunity of bringing a matter before the House which I would like to explain. A question arose and was agitated through the country, being taken up by the Manu-

facturers' Association and the press, as to whether the ruling of our department with reference to the admission of materials for the construction of the Detroit tunnel was more liberal than that of the United States department. The department thought that we had sufficient assurance in the instructions of the United States government to warrant us in what we were doing and that we were perfectly safe. However, the hon. member for West Kent (Mr. Clements) and the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshiitt) took that view, and subsequently, I think, the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) thought that there might be a possible doubt. We did not so think, but in deference to their remarks, and with a view to putting the matter beyond question, I asked the commissioner to again inquire of the Treasury Department, although I did not like to do so as it seemed to imply that their other letter was not sufficiently plain. The following correspondence has been exchanged between the two departments :
Division of Customs.
Treasury Department, Office of the Secretary, Washington, June 24, 1908. Hon. John McDougald,
Canadian Commissioner of Customs, Ottawa, Canada,
Sir,-I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of-the 18th instant, relative to the free entry of materials for use in the construction of the tunnel between Canada and the United: States at Detroit, Michigan.
The department's letter of March 13 last to the collector of customs at Detroit, a correct copy of which is set forth in your letter, is correctly interpreted by you as authorizing the free entry of all materials to be used in the tunnel whether under water or on the American shore, except materials used above ground on the open approach to the tunnel.
Respectfully,
(Sgd.) J. B. REYNOLDS, Assistant Secretary.
No inclosure.
Department of Customs, Ottawa, June 18, 1908. The Assistant Secretary of the Treasury, Washington, D.C.
Sir,-I have the honour to state that the customs tariff of Canada (1907) contains the following provision for free entry of materials for international bridge and tunnels, viz.:-
590. Materials to be used in Canada for the construction of bridges and tunnels crossing the boundary between the United States and Canada, when similar materials are admitted free under similar circumstances into the United States, under regulations prescribed by the Minister of Customs. Free.
Under this provision the contractors for the ' Detroit River Tunnel' between Detroit, Michigan, and Windsor, Ontario, are now making free entries of their materials for the whole covered portion of the tunnel on the Canadian side, not including the open approaches.
429i
This department has received a copy of instructions from the Treasury Department on this subject as follows:-	.
Division of Customs.
Treasury Department,
Office of the Secretary, Washington.
41072 C.A.H.
March 13, 1908.

The Collector of Customs,
Detroit, Michigan.
Sir,-The department is in receipt of your letter of the 6th instant, relative to the entry free of duty of tools and materials to be used in the construction of the tunnel between Canada and the United States under the Detroit river.
The matter of the free entry of materials used in the construction of a tunnel between Canada and the United States was considered by the department in connection with the construction of the tunnel between Port Huron, Michigan, and Sarnia, Ontario, and it was decided that all materials brought into the United States for convenience and taken back into the tunnel and used therein should not be regarded as dutiable importations, without regard to the part of the tunnel in which the same were used. Materials used above ground in the approaches to the tunnel on the American shore were held to be subject to the payment of duty. You will be governed accordingly.
Respectfully,
(Sgd.) BEEKMAN WINTHROP, Assistant Secretary.
The Department of Customs understands by jour letter to the collector at Detroit that it covers materials for the entire length of the tunnel on the American side whether under water or on the shore, the open approach to the end of the tunnel alone being excluded. However, a question has been raised and statements made in the House of Commons that under your ruling above quoted, possibly Canadian materials may be only admitted free of United States duty when to be used in that portion of the tunnel which is under the waters of the Detroit river, and not for that portion of the tunnel which is on the mainland beyond the river on the American side.
As the item in our tariff is based and made contingent upon reciprocal action on the part of your government, will you please state if the view this department has taken of your ruling as above mentioned is correct.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
Commissioner of Customs.

speechtext:
The reply from the United States seems to be entirely satisfactory as establishing their understanding of the ruling. It is a pity that the same explicitness was not had months or maybe years ago, as in that way a great deal of unnecessary discussion would have been saved. This meaning of the regulations being established, can the department in any way use its influence with the contractors to see that Canadian manufacturers and Canadian labour get a really fair show in the purchase of supplies? Is it possible for the department to use any influence in that
33S27

way, as the tunnel seems to be about equally divided between the two countries in point of distance?

maintopic: SUPPLY-DUTY ON MATERIALS FOR INTERNATIONAL TUNNELS.
speechtext: If I may refer to a previous debate, the contractors pointed out In letters which were submitted to the House that $160,000 or $170,000 worth of material had been purchased in Canada. I also read letters from them in which they said they had asked Canadian cement manufacturers to tender, but these manufacturers, for some reason or other, appeared not to have been anxious, as they declined in some cases and in no case had they taken the trouble to personally interview the contractors. It cannot be expected that the interests of a merchant will be looked after if he will not take some trouble himself ; and certainly, where there are to be such large purchases to be made, they seem to have been lacking in that respect. I have no doubt that under the provisions of the tariff we will get an amount of revenue on goods imported from the United States for use in the open approaches on the Canadian side, and I have no doubt either that our manufacturers are in a position, this being reciprocal, to secure a portion of the business of supplying materials for the tunnel on the American side ; as they have an equal opportunity to compete with the Americans on the American side, as the provision is reciprocal. Therefore, I have no doubt, if our cement manufacturers are now in such a position that they have a surplus, they will be able to do business. Of course, we are not in a position to force anything to be done.

The material for the open approaches on both sides is dutiable; our cement manufacturers would not, I think, stand a chance for anything beyond. Our producers being protected with a very large duty on cement, I think that all the cement used in the open approaches on our side will go to our own people. Another point that was raised was that American workmen were being employed and that Canadian workmen were not getting an opportunity. I have been told that employment has been given to all Canadians who make application, and that many thousands of dollars have been paid to Canadian workmen. I can imagine that to be the case. A work such as that is not one in which a great many men may desire to engage, because it is considered somewhat hazardous-at any rate, as a heavy work. I mention this because it was thought that there had been some discrimin-Mr. FOSTER.

The right hon. gentleman knows perfectly well that the hon. member for Brandon would not have been allowed to have made the statements contained in the telegram if he had been in his place in the House. Again I would say to the right hon. gentleman that he will find, at pages 13495 and 13500, the statement made by me that I am not responsible for any one of these statements but that every one is contained in a written document obtained from the Department of the Interior. I wish to direct the attention of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance to the following despatch from Paris which appeared in the newspapers on the 16th inst:
A despatch from Paris says the following explanation is being made of the delay m the approval of the Franco-Canadian convention: When the Canadian parliament passed the new tariff law in 1906 it 'omitted to mention in the schedule of the most favoured^ nations and used as a basis in the negotiations the name of Switzerland, which enjoys such treatment under the treaty with Great Britain of 1865. The slip was not discovered until the convention had passed the chamber, when Switzerland brought her claim to the notice of England. The French deputies, being too late to do anything in tbeir own house, worked upon the senators for the departments of Centre Jura, where the silk and watch-rn aking interests are strong, and thus the opposition began. It is argued that these trades wore among those for which concession had been most 'boasted of and how that 'Switzerland was to share the benefits the value of the concessions fell to the ground. Thereupon the powerful agricultural protectionist party arose in turn ito reproach the' government, saying if they had been silent against the large favours given to Canadian agriculture it was because other French industries were said to 'be ben-fited in return, but if there was to be no just equivalent elsewhere they also objected to the concessions.
The government is as anxious as ever to conclude the treaty with Canada, but it will hesitate to commit itself to condition's framed under a misconception, for which France is not responsible.
The ' Times' ' Paris correspondent believes it is possible to overcome the opposition of

the protectionists and that the Franco-Cana-dian treaty will be ratified in October.
I do not understand some of the details set forth in this despatch, but it seems to imply some default on the part of this government in presenting the measure to parliament, or in the tariff of 1906. I would ask whether there is anything in the despatch, and especially whether there is anything in the suggestion that the delay in the ratification of the treaty is due to any default on the part of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not aware that the delay is in any respect due to any default on the part of Canada, nor am I aware that anybody claims such is the case. There is no doubt that the opposition which has been raised in the French legislative bodies to the treaty, is to some extent due to the special interests referred to which no doubt find that as other favoured nations have to receive the benefits of that treaty they do not get as much advantage from it as they would like to. But beyond that I do not quite see the meaning of the despatch. There is no doubt that the silk trade and possibly the watch trade would receive a greater concession if we could exclude other nations from the benefit of this treaty and give it to France alone. It is not in our power to do that and I have no doubt there is some foundation for the statement that the representations of these interests have had a good deal to do with the delay. I am not aware of anybody alleging that anything has been done on the part of Canada that has caused delay.
The minister has no doubt seen the despatch ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes I suppose it is the same despatch I have seen.

What I do not understand is that it refers to some omission on the part of Canada :
When the Canadian parliament passed the new tariff law in 1906 it omitted to mention in the schedule of the most favoured nations and used as a basis in the negotiations the name of Switzerland.
The language is not quite clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Our tariff Act does not profess to give a list of favoured nation countries. It has been more or less a matter of debate as respects some countries and we have not felt at liberty to give any list of them in the tariff Act. We have from time to time given the best list we could and sometimes the lists have not been absolutely in harmony. For some years there was some doubt about the position of Switzerland and I think it will be found that Switzerland did not in former years claim the favoured nation treatment. No case arose as to which she felt called up-Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
on to assert that position and it was difficult to determine foir the time just exactly what was the correct list. When the treaty was being presented to this House we deemed it proper to ask from the imperial authorities-inasmuch as this obligation arose under old treaties they had made, and not under modern treaties in which Canada was consulted-we deemed it proper to ask from the imperial authorities a list of the favoured nation countries as they were determined on by the foreign office, and in that list Switzerland appeared, although in some of the previous lists I think Switzerland did not appear. The matter was not a subject of any special consideration and the tariff Act did not in itself purport to give any list of favoured nations.
(BORDEN. Has there been any discussion in the French chambers which would throw any light upon the question ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think there was an impression that Switzerland would not be entitled to favoured nation treatment. We were at one time under the impression ourselves-the point not having been directly raised-that Switzerland was not included. No doubt the fact that Switzerland was one of the favoured nations has something to do with the antagonism which has been raised in the French senate, but I am not aware that anybody alleges that it was due to any default on the part of the Canadian government.

What seems to be underlying it is that during the negotiation of the treaty the French negotiators had the idea that Switzerland was not on the most favoured nation list, and so would not participate. When it passed the chamber of deputies in France the same impression prevailed. But, when afterwards it came out, (probably when the application was made by Switzerland to Great Britain) that feature was imported anew into the ratification and because of that the treaty has not been ratified in the French senate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is quite possible. Of course, we ourselves had some doubts in regard to Switzerland, but the occasion had not arisen for us to come to a deter-' mination on the question. But I think it is safe to assume that the able members of the diplomatic staff in Paris were not dependent on any information they might receive from us in respect to the treaties. A moment's thought will suggest to my hon. friend that the very able men who look after these matters in the foreign offices in the courts of Europe are well furnished with copies of all treaties and with able persons to understand and interpret them. Although some persons may have had the impression that Switzerland was not in-

eluded, I cannot imagine that the diplomatic officers in Paris were in the dark on the subject. At any rate, they had access to every paper and document on the subject to which we had access.

I would like to ask the Minister of Agriculture in reference to a statement made in the House the other day that the quarantine regulations in reference to sheep going to the United States applies only to breeding sheep. There is a large trade in Ontario with sheep and lambs which are sent to Buffalo, and I would like to know whether the regulation applies to them.
The information which we have received from the United States authorities distinctly states that the regulation applies to breeding sheep.
Only?
It does not use the word only, but as it reads it does not seem to apply to any others. However, we are in communication with the United States authorities on the subject.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I would like to bring to the attention of the House a matter which should be of a good deal of interest to every hon member, as I know it is to the general public; that is, the amount of wind wasted here in long speeches. In the first session that I was in this House, I was struck by the fact that there was a great deal said that might better be left unsaid, as far as educating the general public or influencing the House was concerned, and I have been strengthened in that belief every session since, and more than ever this session. A short time ago, after the discussion on the Elections Act, I ran over ' Hansard ' and calculated the number of columns which each member had spoken in the House, and gave the results to the House. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) said that the government side had been responsible for far more of the contents of ' Hansard ' than the opposition side, and claimed that if we took the session from the beginning we would find that to be the case. Since then I have taken the trouble to go through the ' Unrevised Hansard ' and figure out as carefully as I could the amount of space which each man has occupied from the beginning of the session to last Wednesday night. If I had continued the calculation for the days since that date, the result would look very much worse for the gentlemen on the other side of the House. I
may say that I have not included any of the little questions asked across the House, which would not occupy more than an inch or so of * Hansard,' but have only taken what might be termed set speeches. Where a speech occupied a number of columns with a little piece over, I dropped the little piece. Any one who looks through ' Hansard ' will find that I have been as fair as 1 could possibly be. From my examination I find that since the beginning of the session to Wednesday night last the government are responsible for 4,004 columns of ' Hansard ' and the opposition for 4,636, a difference of 632 columns against the opposition ; and considering that there are only half as many men on the opposition side as on the government side, we shall have to give them credit for a great deal more long-windedness, versatility and loquaciousness than we on this side possess. I would not wish to hurt any one's feelings, but I am sorry to say that the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) is by far the worst sinner of all. He is responsible for 624 columns. His leader comes next with 434 The five who contribute the most largely are the hon. member for North Toronto, with 624 columns, the hon. leader of the opposition with 434 columns, the Minister of the Interior with 3S8 columns, the Prime Minister with 269 columns, and the Minister of Finance with 266 columns. When we consider that the twelve cabinet ministers in the House have a great deal to answer-
Hear, hear.

I did not say to answer for ; I said a great many questions to answer. It is true they have a great deal to answer for, and so have we all. But considering that they have all the government business to introduce and explain, and questions both wise and unwise to answer, I think it is rather strange that the twelve cabinet ministers have not occupied as much space as eight of the gentlemen on the other side of the House. I do not know that it would be of interest to the House that I should read this whole list, though I would like to see it go on ' Hansard.' As I went along I took note of those who had made the longest speeches of this session, with the following result: Dr. Roche (Marquette), 63 columns ; Colonel Worthington (Sherbrooke), 50 ; Sir Frederick Borden, (Kings, N.S.), 41 ; Mr. Alcorn (Prince Edward), 41 ; Dr. Schaffner, (Souris), 41 ; Mr. Oliver (Edmonton), 40 ; Mr. Aylesworth (North York), 39 ; Mr. Miller (South Grey) 37 ; Mr. Crawford (Portage la Prairie), 36; Mr. Guthrie (South Wellington), 34; Mr. fibster (North Toronto), 35 twice ; Mr. Monk, (Jacques Cartier), 34 ; Mr. Lewis, (West Huron), 33 ; Mr. Boyce (West Al-goma), 33 ; Mr. Armstrong (East Lambton), 29 ; Mr. McCool (Nipissing), 29 ; Hon. Now, I hope we will all take this into our serious consideration and see if we cannot adopt some means by which every hon. member can place his ideas before the House in fewer words, throwing out a great deal of what is useless. For there is no doubt that, as every member of the House knows, a great deal that is said in this House might well be left unsaid. It does not convince anybody here, and it does not interest anybody outside. It would be greatly to the advantage of hon. members who have to sit here and listen and to the great, long-suffering public outside if speeches here were shorter.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Kennedy), I think, has given the best justification of the opposition that could possibly be given. What is the occasion of the hon. gentleman's speech this afternoon? The misdeeds of the opposition. And what is the occasion of the long speeches of the opposition? The misdeeds of the government. Well, as the misdeeds of the government exceed the misdeeds of the opposition a thousandfold, the opposition might well have extended their speeches to a much greater average than the hon. gentleman has given without laying themselves open to criticism.

I presume that this is the last dying speech and confession of the patriarch from British Columbia who has just addressed us. I think it would have been much more fitting if he had delivered this spech in a caucus of his friends and had endeavoured to persuade them to bring in the Bills which they foreshadowed in the speech from the Throne without waiting until the dying hours of the session. It would be more fitting if he were to warn them of the effects of bringing in such an obnoxious Bill as the Election Act amendment which we found necessary to fight at every stage, even to the extent of stopping the voting of Supply. This was the only power we could oppose to the overwhelming majority of the government and prevent the outrage upon the country that they were attempting.

I had intended, in company with two or three other hon. members, to take up a little more at length than I shall be able to do certain matters in connection with the Department of Militia and Defence. But at this time of the session, with almost everybody away, when my friends who were to have taken part in this discussion have been obliged to leave, I must content myself with saying much less than I should have done. In fact, I think all I can do now is to ask some questions. In the first place, I do not know whether the minister has explained to the House the transaction in lands at Niagara. If I am not misinformed, a considerable tract of land has been bought at Niagara for the purposes of a permanent camp. If the minister has already explained that transaction I am not aware of that explanation.

I do not know that any reference has been made to this transaction. As every one knows, there is an old fort at Niagara which is one of the landmarks of Canadian history. Some years ago the question arose as to whether we should be able to continue to hold camp there, as we have been doing for years, because the camp ground was reported to be too small. The rifle rauge there is not sufficient for the modern rifle. Before constructing a rifle range it was thought desirable to look about and see whether we could not find a more suitable camp somewhere else. Several places were

examined, one in Simcoe was favourably reported upon. But when we tried to acquire the land the price was put up, and it was thought undesirable to go on with the purchase. Later on, the military staff of my department suggested the desirability of acquiring more land at Niagara adjacent to the lands already owned by us. I thought this a good idea. There is a very strong feeling in Ontario against abandoning the old historic grounds. General Lake kindly offered to take the matter in hand and had some correspondence, I believe with the authorities of the town of Niagara-on-the-Lake. If I remember correctly, the result of the correspondence was that the mayor of the town was able to procure an option on some 200 acres of land-I have forgottefn the exact arfea : had I known that this matter was coming up I would have brought the papers with me. The price at which the land was offered was very low. A recommendation was made to council and the offer was accepted, and to-day we are the owners of that land. I have no doubt that it was secured at most favourable rates. It was done through the authorities of the town of Niagara-on-the-Lake, which town was naturally very much opposed to the withdrawal of the camp from the old ground and took every means possible to assist the department in procuring the necessary-land at a favourable figure. I cannot tell my hon. friend what the price was, but I know it was a very fair price indeed.
I think the minister must be in a position to tell us what the price is. How long ago was this land bought?
I suppose three months ago, perhaps more.
Has it been paid for?
I think so.
Out of what vote?
The vote of $1,300,000 for ordnance, rifles, lands, etc., capital account.	.
Does the minister know what the price was?
I do not remember.
It seems extraordinary the minister would buy 200 acres of land and not remember approximately the price of the land.

I did not buy the land, it was bought by the officers of my department, or rather it was bought for us by the authorities of the town. I cannot carry those things in my mind, but it seems to me it was somewhere about $80 an acre, but I am speaking from memory.
R If the'minister knew the names of the vendors I could give some idea of the value of the land.
My estimates have gone through, and I have not the papers here ; it was largely peach orchards. I am absolutely certain it was a great bargain.

I am not taking any exception to the buying of lands for military purposes if it is necessary and if it is properly conducted, but it seems to me a transaction of that extent-buying 200 acres at the rate of $80-is a pretty large transaction without parliament knowing anything of it. The vote is for the purchase of ordnance, arms, lands for military purposes, stores, clothing, etc. I have the same objection to this as I have expressed to other votes, that under this resolution the minister could spend a million dollars for lands without parliament knowing anything of it.
I shall get the information in ten minutes ; I am anxious to give it.

I understand the minister has made a contract for the manufacture of bayonets in the country, for some 52,000, and that the contract has been made with the Ross Rifle Company. Has that contract ever been laid before parliament?
I think, so.
It was before the Public Accounts Committee.

It is the right of this parliament to have information with reference to such contracts. By what authority did the minister enter into a contract for a quarter of a million dollars without having brought it before parliament? All the information I have gained has been by means of questions In the House. But as it appears, without any discussion in parliament or any approval of the plan by parliament, the minister has entered into a contract with the Ross Rifle Company for the manufacture of 52,000 bayonets at $5.25 per bayonet complete. That amounts to over a quarter of a million dollars, and had it not been for some questions asked in the House parliament would have had no knowledge of what had been done. Does not the minister think that in entering into a contract for $250,000 he should have been specially authorized by parliament upon information detailed to the House? It is not a small transaction, it is a large transaction, and in this case has to do with the effectiveness of a force. If we look at current prices, I think I am entirely within the mark in saying that $5.25 is an extremely high price for bayonets. I find that the price of the bayonet and scabbard

complete at the War Office for use with the rifle of the British force cost 9s. 8id., that is just $2.32.
At what time?

In 1897.
Sir FREDERICK? BORDEN. Yes.

And at the present time I fail to find that the price of the bayonet is appreciably higher. I find the United States bayonet used by the United States troops and attached to their rifle costs even less than that.
How does the hon. member arrive at the cost of the United States bayonet?
A statement by one of its military officers.
Manufactured by the United States itself?
Exactly, as this is manufactured at a factory for which we have provided every dollar of the working capital.
Not at all.
And in advance of making-
We do nothing of the kind.

And in reference to this very contract, in which we advance 75 per cent of the total value of it before we get the bayonet. The very same article, if I am informed correctly, is in this contract as in the rifle contract, that we advance 75 per cent of the cost, which is three-quarters of $5.25.
We do not advance a dollar.
The minister need not say
The hon. gentleman need not misstate.
I am not misstating.
He is absolutely misstating it, and he knows it. You know it perfectly well; you know you are stating what is not a fact. You are doing it deliberately.
I am stating what is absolutely the fact.
You are not.
He has no right to speak to me in that way.

The bon. gentleman must not think he can talk to Mr. FOSTER.
people and insinuate and make improper and unfair statements, without getting his answer back.

Every time this year that any person ihas attempted to criticise this hon. gentleman he has been blackguarded by him for doing so, across the floor of the House. He does not stop criticism that way. Let him bring his contract and place it on the table of the House, and I think I will be able to show him out of the contract that he does exactly in this case what he did in the Ross rifle case, that he advances 75 per cent before the articles furnished to the department.

We do not advance in the case of the Ross Rifle contract, and that is what I say, and the hon. gentleman knows it. We give 75 per cent after 75 per cent of the work is done.
(Mr. FOSTER. What I said, and the minister cannot crawl out of it in that way, is that before a single rifle was furnished to this government they had advanced 75 per cent of the contract price of the rifle, and he knows that is absolutely true.
No, what the hon. gentleman said was that we supplied the working capital for the company, which is not correct; and he said that every dollar of the money was paid before any work was done.
I did not.
Then how can the hon. gentleman say that we advanced the capital ?

I did not say before it was done. I said before the rifles were delivered. That is what I said, and the ' Hansard ' will show it. and if the minister thinks it is not so we can refer to the ' Hansard ' report.
Then there is nothing in your statement.
There is something in the statement, as I think, though my hon. friend may think there |is nothing.
Nothing at all.

So I think it will be found that this is the condition, that the government is to advance the money expended on all bayonets, scabbards, parts thereof and materials therefor, to be delivered in any year up to 75 per cent of the price. That is exactly the wording of the contract in the case of the Ross rifle. Now in reference to the Ross rifle, what took place ? This state of things, that although an order was given at a certain time, the advances were thousands of dollars and hundreds of thousands of dollars over aud against these rifles, before a single one, or at least before the sale of rifles called for in

any one contract, was delivered. I have the figures here, they have been so often placed before the House that it does not seem necessary for me to do it again, but if the minister makes it necessary, I shall read the record out of his own mouth.
I find that the first contract for the Boss rifles was given March 27, 1902, for delivery in the calendar year of 1903.
And the contract with the Ross Rifle Company only allows him to make an advance for the space of one year during which they are to be delivered. Here then is the date of the contract, March 27, 1902, for 12,000 rifles. Well, Sir, there was not a rifle delivered until August, 1905. Then 1,000; and in October 1905, 3,000; and in December, 2,000. And yet if you will take the companion statement given by himself you will find that on August 6, 1905, $506,000 had been paid out by this government to the Ross Rifle Company, and at that time he had not more than 1,000 rifles delivered.
We have got them now.

You have got them now, and that is the way the minister thinks a contract is kept. Now I say that the same reading is in the articles of the contract for bayonets as was in the article of the Ross rifle contract, the very same terms; therefore, we may look for the very same noncarrying out. Now does the minister want me to read any more of these figures as to the immense sums of money that were paid, first, before a single rifle was delivered, and afterwards, before one-tenth of the number practically called for by that contract, had been delivered. Now it appears that in this matter the minister has given the extravagant price of $5.25 for bayonets, that he hag added to that the same condition that was in the Ross rifle contract, namely, that he can advance up to 75 per cent of the material and labour involved, before a single rifle bayonet is delivered.
But after the work is done, and after the materials are there.
-Not after the work is done, necessarily; after certain material is bought and after certain work is done, or before any work is done, if the material is there.	.

It is only on material.
Mr. FOSTER And that may be advanced to hundreds of thousands of dollars before he has a single finished rifle. These are the facts ; That the minister gave orders, under the Ross rifle contract, for delivery of a certain number of rifles at various times; that the contract was not lived up to; that the minister advanced, for instance, in this case $506,000 before he had more than 1,000 rifles; that this contract is completed upon
exactly the same plan; it takes power to advance in exactly the same way. Therefore what will take place in what took place in the other case, that you actually give into these gentlemen's hands a working capital for the contract you give them, and for which you pay them. Now I was going on to say that the price of the United States bayonet is $1.43, that is what it costs. When the minister says that it is manufactured in government works, what are these down here at Quebec? What did you give to the Ross Rifle Company ? You gave them in perpetuity almost nineteen and a half acres of government land on the Plains of Abraham. That is what he gave them, for $1 a year. That is, he gave them their site. What next did he give them? He gave them outside of what they get in the city of Quebec-that is their own matter, an exemption from taxation-he gave them this contract on which he advances 75 per cent, as I have stated.
I say we do not.

Before the minister had a single rifle made and delivered, this government had paid out nearly $500,000; and before he had more than 1,000, they had paid in actual cash $506,000. The very same thing went on. This means that you are giving them your working capital. Suppose the minister's contract was that he paid them for their rifles when they delivered them; then, for every dollar's worth of material they bought they would have to furnish their own capital, for every hour of labour they would have to pay for it out of their own capital and they would get no money from the government until they had delivered the goods. But, in this case they get $506,000 out of the government before they deliver one single rifle. Is that not furnishing the working capital ? Take that out of the contract and they would have to furnish all the capital, find all the material and pay all the labour.
They did furnish it.
The minister furnished $506,000.
No, paid it on account of work done.
That is shown by his own answer.
That is not so.

And it is shown as well by the accounts. The minister knows the position that was taken by the Auditor General. In the course of time the Auditor General had to sit down on the minister and refuse to pay. He refused to pay because there was a constant advance of government funds before there was delivery of

the goods that were to be paid for, and he objected to it. The minister knows that and the minister knows that he had to go to council and get it to extend the time of the contract and so get payment in the end from the Auditor General. To sum up, first, a contract was made for $250,000 and this parliament does not know about it until to-day. In the second place the minister pays $5.25 for each bayonet when the bayonet supplied by the government of Great Britain is purchased for $2.92 and when the United States bayonet, made in the government works, it is said, costs $1.43.
I would need some better evidence than the hon. gentleman's statement as to that fact.
Does the minister say that the United States bayonet does not cost that ?
I do not believe it.
The minister does not ?
No.
Well, if the minister will ask his own officers lie will find out that what I tell him is the fact.
The hon. gentleman has been around my officers ?
Around your offices ? Are they your offices ?	.
Officers, I said.
Are they your offices or are they your officers ?
They are more mine than they are your's.
At present. I know you think you own the whole thing but I do not think you do. I have a perfect right to go to your offices.

Certainly and I have no doubt the hon. gentleman has been there just as he was in the Department of the Interior and the Department of Marine and Fisheries running around after the accountants to try to find out what is going on.
I absolutely deny such and both of these assertions and demand a retraction of them. .
I will not retract them.

speechtext: It is customary to accept an hon. member's statement.

Certainly. I was informed and believed until this minute that the hon. gentleman had been doing what I have stated. I am bound, as I did on a former occasion, to accept the hon. gentleman's statement that he did not.
Then the hon. gentleman, having on a former occasion had to take back such assertions, ought to have learned something from his experience.
I may have something to say about the former occasion.
If the hon. gentleman wants to say something more let him say it now. Let him come right out with it.
Go on.

I have not done myself the honour of being in the minister's department. I do not know that I have been in it for four years, but if I wanted to go I would have a perfect right to go. The hon. gentleman has called them his offices. I do not think they are his.
They are in occupation by me at the present time.
Yes, unfortunately for this country they are.
In your opinion.

That is my opinion. Now I was going on to say when I was thus rudely interrupted by the minister, for which interruption he has had to make a retraction, that if he did not know he should have known and that if he will ask his own officers I think he will-
My officers.
Yes.	.
Oh, a few minutes ago they were not my officers.
They are your officers in occupation.
The hon. gentleman found fault with me for calling them my officers.

I will declare that they are his in occupation and humour him in that respect. However, if he will ask his officers-his by virtue of occupation for a short time only-he will find the records in his own department as to the price of the United States bayonet. I find here in
