my notes, that, according to a letter from F. C. Ainsworth, Military secretary, acting secretary of war, August 25, 1906, and over his signature, the cost of the magazine rifle is given in the report of the Ordnance Department of the United States as $14.90, cleaning rod 24 cents and bayonet $1.42, the whole cost being $16.57. I base my statement as to the cost of the United States rifle on that authority. The minister says it is not true.
I do not know what the hon. gentleman is reading from.
X am reading from my notes.
I thought so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: A letter from *Mr. Ainsworth ?
Yes, this is taken from a letter of Mr. Ainsworth.
To whom?
To the department.
To my department ?
By courtesy-your department.
Thank you.
There is an immense difference between that and. a contract of this kind.

In the first place the hon. gentleman finds fault with the fact that a contract has been entered into of $250,000 or thereabouts without the special authority of parliament. I may say at once in answer to the hon. gentleman that it has not been customary to lay contracts of this kind on the table or to ask the special permission of parliament for ithean^ Th.e hofci. gentleman, himself, in 1896, bought $1,000,000 worth of rifles and bayonets in England. He did not submit any contract, although I suppose they were bought on contract, to this House. He asked this House to vote $1,000,000 to enable him to buy rifles and bayonets.
Yes.

I asked this House last year to vote $1,300,000 for the purpose of buying rifles and bayonets and various other things. In 1903 or 1904, I came to this House and stated the policy of the government with reference to the building up of the reserve of arms, ordnance, clothing, and all the various things required for the militia and I stated that that vote would be repeated probably for five years in succession. That vote has been repeated and out of that vote the materials, arms and
other things have been bought exactly as stated to parliament at the time, and in each year, in the Auditor General's Report and in the militia report, a full account has been given of what has been done. In regard to. this contract there was no secret. Information was asked in this House months ago and was given. The contract was entered into on May 4, and a statement was made in the House. I thought a copy of the contract had been laid on the table, but if not I am sorry as I intended it should be. The authority of parliament had been given quite as much in this case as in the case in which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) purchased a million dollars worth of rifles and bayonets. The hon. gentleman states the price is altogether too high, and as authority he quotes a letter from somebody to the department stating that the price of the United States bayonet is $1.43. I doubt that. He says it is made in the ordnance factory in the United States, and if so, that represents the bare cost and not the cost as it would be if manufactured in a business establishment by a business concern. That is well known both in the United States and in England. I find that the hon. gentleman himself purchased bayonets in England in 1896 and a portion of the rifles and bayonets he bought were bought from the War Office direct and another portion through the War Office from the trade. The portion purchased from the trade in England in 1896 cost 15 shillings and 5 pence halfpenny, including all expenses, or $3.71. Applying the duty which is now imposed on bayonets to that price the cost would be $4.46. I find that at the time the hon. gentleman made his purchases he happened to go into the market at a very favourable moment, and that he got a reduction of about 124 per cent below the regular prices. When a factory begins the manufacture of armament of any kind there is always added to the estimated cost an estimate to cover initial expenses at the outset of manufacturing. It so happens that at the time General Lake made these purchases for the hon. gentleman in England the time had passed during which that 121 per cent was maintained, and he got a reduction upon his rifles and bayonets of about 124 per cent. Therefore if you add that 124 per cent to the $4.46 paid you will see that the price will be considerably higher than the $5.25 upon which this contrast is based. That is called the initial expense which is reckoned for in all contracts of this kind. $5.25 being the contract price, $4.46 being the cost which the hon. gentleman paid for the bayonet; it would give 79 ceDts to cover the initial cost of expenditure to provide for manufacture. I think the hon. gentleman is misinformed as to the cost of the bayonet at the War Office to-day, because I have here the latest quotation of the price of bayonet and scabbard in England and the cost of 25,844 bayonets accordng to ord-

nance factories account-that is at the ordnance not the trade outside-is $2.02, and the cost of 688 scabbards, 3 shillings and 3 pence halfpenny or 80 cents, making $2.82; the departmental expenses, 154, freight 14, making a total of S3.ll! cents, and applying duty to this you will get about $4. The ordnance factories, prices for bayonets and scabbards given above do not include initial expense. The average difference between ordnance factories price and the price to the trade paid by the British government is approximately 35 per cent. This does not include any charge for initial expenditure. If you add that on it will bring it to $5,024 cents which leaves 224 cents per bayonet and scabbard for the initial expense on a contract for 52,000, equal to $11,700, which I think is not an extravagant allowance for the Initial expense in a matter of this kind. In the case of rifles it is different, but in the case of bayonets the government is absolutely the only customer the contractor has so that when this contract is finished that is the end of it and unless some provision is made to the contractor for initial expense he would be very likely to make a loss, a thing which I do not think anybody desires. But the department took the precaution to ask somebody else. They asked the only other people in Canada who could do work of this kind. They asked the Ottawa Car Company to tender on this contract and the Ottawa Car Company did tender and if I remember correctly their tender was $5.45 so that the contract was given to the lowest tenderer. I believe that from all points of view the contract was a fair one. As to the quantity ordered-52,000 rifles are under order from the Ross Rifle Company, and it was therefore necessary to have 52,000 bayonets and a contract was entered into for the delivery of that number within threie' years.
The hon. gentleman will see that it is not $260,000, or whatever the amount of the contract may be, in one year ; but it is spread over three years. So that it is not such an alarming thing ; and of course it is absolutely necessary that we should have the bayonets in order that the rifles may be distributed to the troops as early as possible. The hon. gentleman has taken exception to this contract on the ground that it is similar to the Ross rifle contract, in authorizing advances up to 75 per cent.
We had that matter very fully threshed out in this House when the Ross rifle was under discussion. I stated then, and I repeat now, that in a contract of this kind, encouraging a new industry in this .country, it was absolutely necessary that reasonable encouragement should be given to the contractor. He had to put up an expensive building and put in expensive machinery, and it was only fair that reasonable advances should be made to him as the work progressed. In England payments are always made in advance. The war office itself, if we gave Sir FREDERICK BORDEN.
them an order, would require the whole or nearly the whole of it to be paid for in advance. It does not seem to me to be unreasonable that this company should be paid, not in advance-I do not know that the hon. gentleman wished to misstate the fact, and if I gave the impression that I thought he did, I apologize ; but I understood him to say that we paid this money in advance and supplied the company with its working capital. That is not true. What is done is this. After materials have been bought, after work has been done, a reliable man, a chartered accountant approved of by the Auditor General, goes and takes stock and examines all the vouchers and all the bills for all the material, and ithe books showing the labour expended, and upon that data furnishes the department with a statement on which 75 per cent of the value of the rifles is paid. The hon. gentleman makes a great point of the fact that considerable money at one time was advanced before any rifles were received. That is quite true. There were difficulties in the matter of the construction of the rifle and the delay was quite as much due to the officers of the department as to the company itself. The company was anxious to deliver a satisfactory rifle. The inspector was anxious that a satisfactory rifle should be delivered, and the inspector representing the department on the one hand and the officers of the company on the other hand worked together with a view to making certain changes in the mechanism to bring about the desirable result of delivering to the department and the country a first-i'ate rifle. This caused a certain amount of delay. I think for nearly a year there were no deliveries, but the w'ork was going on. Four or five hundred men were working. We had the evidence of the chartered accountant before the Public Accounts Committee that out of $1,100,000 expended, $900,000 or about that sum was upon labour employed in the factory. So, in view of the fact that this was a new industry employing 500 men, and that it was in accordance with the policy laid down by the War Office that we should be as independent as possible in matters of this kind, it seems to me that there should be no serious complaint made against the department for extending reasonable leniency. The hon. gentleman says that we violated the contract. The hon. gentleman ought to know better. We did not violate the contract. My late deputy was a lawyer of good, standing, and he passed these different demands for advances as they came in, and it never occurred to him, nor to anybody else but the Auditor General, that these payments should be limited to a given year. The Auditor General took a different view. It was quite proper for him to do so if he chose ; he did it conscientiously. At my suggestion the matter was submitted to the Department of Justice, who ruled that the action of my department 1 was in accordance with the contract. Then

it was that the Auditor General said : Then X must ask council to approve of the extension of time ; and that was done. It was perfectly proper. It ought to have been done before, and I do not see that the department is liable to any very great censure for that.

On the 4th of May, 1908.

Why would not the hon. gentleman give the same privilege to a manufacturer who is making material for the government that he would to a manufacturer who is making material Sir FREDERICK BORDEN.
for the public? Why should not the manufacturer of bayonets, for instance, have the benefit of this provision as to duty as well as the woollen manufacturer, the cotton manufacturer or the sewing machine manufacturer?

In the first place, the minister will see there is a great difference. The government treats no woollen manufacturer as it treats this manufacturer of rifles and bayonets. It does not give them a free site in perpetuity-

But towns do.
Mr. FOSTER-and it does not give them an advance on the price of goods, which advance, in this case, amounted to a very large sum before a single rifle was delivered. Let us reason that out for a moment. The general manufacturer has to select his material and buy it, to select his labour and pay it. He has to go through the whole process from the raw material up to the finished article. He then ihas to have that pass inspection, he ships it and the delivery is made. Then he gets his payment and not before. By this bayonet contract the man who manufactures buys the material and hires his men, but he pays for that material and for that labour out of the advance of 75 per cent and that is actually, to that extent, working capital which is provided for him by the government. He buys his material for a certain consignment of rifles or of bayonets and he puts his labour on it. He buys his material for two or three months, whatever are the terms, he puts his labour on that and he works it up and all the time his labour is working on it and bringing it towards the perfected instrument whatever it is, the bayonet or the rifle, he is receiving 75 per cent of the contract price which is, I think we will all admit, very close to the actual cost of the finished article, leaving the other 25 per cent for profit to the manufacturer. Therefore it is plain enough that whatever you may call it the man is really getting by his advance the working capital that is necessary for him to buy his material and employ his labour. You can always buy from the war office. The war office would be very willing to accommodate themselves to and work in co-operation with the government of Canada or any other colony. When we bought war material it was made what we call a rush order as sometimes has to be done. We wanted that $1,000,000 worth or more as quickly as possible. The war office provided us with one-half of those rifles and the small arms factory at Birmingham supplied the remaining half. Arrangements could have been made just as well, to-day as then with the British government by which the rifles and bayonets as well could have been provided, in whole or in part, by the ordnance department and perhaps in part by the dif-

ferent factories of small arms in Birmingham and other places. It is true that the outside manufacturer charges more man the imperial government does. It is also true that when the imperial government requires the installation of additional machinery for making ordnances for itself it allows. for a certain period of time, a little larger price. I think the allowance was about 10 shillings in the ease of the small arms company at Birmingham.

The difference between us is not great. The average then according to the minister's paper would be less than my average, $20,774 for the 40,000. There is no doubt the minister could have made very much the same kind of an arrangement with the British war office and with the manufacturer's of arms, and I do not think you will find there has been a very large appreciation in the price. What does the minister's Ross rifle cost him ? It costs him without the bayonet, about $28 to $29 per rifle.

No, he has to take in everything in connection with the cost. There is the amount he has paid for changes and other improvements, that is he has undertaken to experiment upon a rifle which it has taken himi from 1902 to 1908 to get into what he thinks just now is a 4304

There may be but that is what these rifles have cost up to the present time, and that need not have been added to I the cost if the minister had bought in Great Britain. He has had to pay $30,967 for changes and improvements, $76,580 for inspection, rentals, &c., and $26,237 for gauges so that the total payment for the 40,000 rifles, according to his own answer, is $1,138,784 which brings the cost up to $28.47. Then he has no bayonet. If he adds the price of the bayonet $5.25 and there will bp inspection and other charges for this, he will have $33.72 which his rifle and bayonet-will cost him, whereas from the war office, the whole'thing complete cost us $20,774 each for 40,000 rifles. The difference between $20,774 and $33.72 represents just about the difference in the price that we have to pay. The same arrangement could, I think, have been made and the same relative saving.

Yes.
Then why not buy woollens and cottons there?

I do not think you can ever go on the same system and rule with reference to the manufacture of arms by a government as you can in respect of the general trade and manufactures of the country ; you may force that argument in, but I do not think it is altogether a fair way of putting it.
With reference to the bayonets, the same thing takes place. The minister could go to the British War Office and buy his bayonets for 9s. 8|d., adding some cost which would bring it up a little, or he could buy them from the small arms factories for about 13s. 2}d. There may be some little cost added to that. Suppose he got the orders about equally placed for that 52,000, it would make an average in the vicinity of $3 per bayonet. - Now he is paying $5.25 per bayonet. It seems to me it would have been a far better policy in the manufacture of both bayonets and rifles to have kept ourselves in exact unison with Great Britain. They have certainly had the greater experience in the manufacture of arms; they have the knowledge and the expert skill ; they are as interested in getting the very best arm for the British service, more interested than probably any other country in the world-certainly they are as much

Interested as we are. We would have had the benefit of uniformity in arms and of the experience and skill and the cost of experimenting by the British government itself. The main argument that has been advanced in favour of the present system is that you wanted to be independent. But the fact is you are not independent now, in the manufacture of the Ross rifle you bring into this country from the United States manufactured parts. In the manufacture of the Ross rifle you bring in from the United States certain manufactured parts. I think we would have been just as independent if we had kept up the connection with the British War Office. Great Britain has command of the sea, and will keep it as long as she is a strong and permanent empire. I do not think there is much doubt as to our being always in a position to get our supplies of arms in that way from Great Britain. We would then keep side by side with the British government in all its improvements, and we would have a uniform arm. Instead of that, the minister went to work and undertook to manufacture a rifle, and it took him years to know what kind of a rifle he wanted. It may have been that the Ross rifle, as Ross brought it here, was a better rifle than it is to-day after it has gone through these experimentations.
It is rather late in the session to go over that question.

I think the hon. gentleman will see that it is hardly fair to repeat this whole debate over again. I have discussed the question-here for an hour or more. It is hardly fair to me ; it is hardly fair to the House at this hour, within a few hours of prorogation, to precipitate the debate anew. All that he has said has been said two or three .times already during this session. Every one of these statements he is making has been answered. I appeal to the hon. gentleman as to whether this is the sort of thing we would expect from an old parliamentarian on the eve of the prorogation of parliament.
I am making my statement with reference primarily to the bayonet contract, and I am arguing from the Ross rifle contract to the bayonet contract.

There is just one point. Reference was made to the primary rifle being better than the present rifle. I may tell him that the rifle that is now in the hands of the soldiers, and which has been condemned, has come through the severest test any rifle has ever passed through, and has proven itself equal to any rifle in the world. It is a question of test.

After all, you are dependent upon the rifle factory here, which is not manufacturing bayonets, and you are Mr. FOSTER.
paying $5.25, when I am certain you could have got those bayonets made by the War Office and by the other companies in Great Britain at a figure somewhere in the neighbourhood of $3 to $3.50 each. As to independence in the matter, why, if war came to-morrow, or any time within two years, or even three years, if it came of a sudden, the factory here could not supply you, it is not able to do it. You would have then to go to the British government and get your supplies in the old country.

For the third or fourth time I must repeat, as briefly as possible, what I have said before as a justification for undertaking to encourage the manufacture of arms in this country. Let me preface that by asking the hon. gentleman :	Why did the government to which he belonged encourage the manufacture of ammunition? It could have been procured more cheaply in England. Why did he do that ? When I came into the office the factory established by the hon. gentleman was manufacturing some
600.000	or 700,000 rounds of ammunition a year. I am happy to say that quantity has been increased from 600,000 to about 10,000,000 or 12,000,000 rounds. The hon. gentleman says we can always get what rifles we want in England. Well, we could not. In the year 1900 I tried to get 10,000 and we could not get 2,000. We did not know what was going to happen in 1900. We had sent 7,000 troops to South Africa armed with 7,000 of our own rifles and had reduced our stock. We wanted more ; we
.tried to get 10,000, and we could not get
2.000	the very moment we wanted them. The hon. gentleman's argument would apply to any manufacture in Canada. I am surprised that an old national policy advocate should stand up here at this day and recommend that we should go on in this manner, being absolutely dependent upon the supply to come from the mother country. The same argument that applies to any manufacture in this country applies with greater force in this case, because this is a question of defence ; it is a vital question, both to this country and to the empire at large. I read the other night-the hon. gentleman was here and heard me- from the blue-books laid before the imperial authorities a year ago, and what did it say ?
No review of the strategical conditions of the British empire, even when suoh a review is limited to the ipurely military aspects of the question, can be undertaken without admitting as a first and fundamental -principle that the maintenance of the empire rests primarily upon supremacy at sea.
Suppose that supremacy was interrupted, as it might be, even temporarily, and communication were cut off between this country and the mother country. It might

happen, it would be very likely to happen, it is possible, it is probable, if a union of any two great powers took place against Great Britain. I do not believe it would be permanent, but it might continue long enough to place us in the greatest peril, and absolutely imperil the connection between this countrj and the mother country. What did this blue-book say further ?
It is most desirable that the area of supply of the warlike store under reference should be _ as wide as possible, and therefore the colonial governments should be urged to arrange for local 'manufacture and provisions, rather than to rely on the resources of the United Kingdom.
There is the answer to the hon. gentleman. If we are to carry out our policy, do our part in defence of this empire, we must be prepared to manufacture, not only the rifles, but the ordnance and ammunition of all kinds, in our own country. That is the best way, no matter what it may cost. The cost must be kept within a reasonable amount. But it cannot be done yet as cheaply as it can in England. The department will carry out that policy so far as the manufacture of ammunition is concerned. We are already manufacturing ammunition in this country as cheaply, after twenty years of experience, as it can be done in England. The time will come when we may be able to manufacture rifles and ordnance as cheaply, but it will be many years. Wre must pay higher prices In the meantime ; labour is dearer. The hon. gentleman says : Oh, but it is not manufactured in Canada after all, you have to get the material outside. That argument would be just as sound and just as strong against almost any factory in Canada. Why, even agricultural implements are manufactured to a considerable extent from materials imported, and have to be. Carriages manufactured in this country are manufactured from imported material. We must creep before we walk. On the policy which the hon. gentleman lays down we would be content to remain in the condition we were in under his administration, and never be able to manufacture for ourselves. I do not believe that is a policy which the people of this country will endorse. I am quite content to leave this contract and to leave the policy in the judgment of the people to say whether It has been wise or whether it has been unwise.

Is the Minister of Public Works making any special provision for more rapid progress on the work in connection with the Geological Survey building? I understand that some of the minor contractors for heating, lighting, &c., are rather slow at their work and that the general work of the building is being interfered with.

That is not the case. The contractor for the building, Mr. Goodwin, is pushing it very rapidly, but the contract for the heating, lighting, fittings, &c., has not yet been let. I stated in the House that I would ask for tenders for the heating, lighting and fittings, but since then representations have been made urging me to push the work forward and I have a proposal from the contractor with reference to the heating, lighting and fittings. The matter is now under consideration. Everything will be done to push forward the building and the progress so far has been as rapid as it possibly eould.
How long before the building will be completed ?

If arrangements can be made so that the subsidiary work of heating, lighting, fittings, &c., can go on concurrently with the main work of the building, I am informed it may be possible to provide for a large number of the specimens in the present museum even during the coming winter. I expect the whole building will be completed next year.

Apart from ,the necessity of protecting the specimens at the geological museum, any one who enters the present museum must see that if a fire

should break out there is great danger of loss of life. A considerable portion of the present museum is made up of buildings attached to the stone building. This shows the necessity of pushing the completion of the geological museum as rapidly as possible.
Mines Branch-investigation of ore deposits and economic minerals; of fuel values of coals and peat of Canada; examination and delimitation of peat hogs, $35,250.

I would like to ask the Minister of Mines (Mr. Templeman) what provision, if any, he has made for Dr. Bell, who, after the death of Dr. Dawson, took on the work for a number of years which Dr. Dawson had done, on the salary that he was getting at the time that Dr. Dawson died. I think that Dr. Bell received no addition at all for the extra work he did from the time of Dr. Dawson's death until the appointment of Mr. Low. It seems .to me that Dr. Bell's service, the length of time in which he has been employed by the department, his world-wide reputation, and the very fact that most of tile work which has been done since in the way of publication and, I am not sure, but most of the work of exploration, has been based upon the work of Dr. Bell previous to that. Anyway, it seems .to me that a man who was neither appointed as director nor definitely told that he would be appointed as director, but who, for a number of years, did the work, and it is somewhat onerous work, ought to have had some recognition. X am not sure whether anything has been done in the way of an increase of salary or by an appropriation for the difference in the salaries, or provision in any other respect. .1 would like to ask the minister if he would inform the House in reference to that ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: He was acting Director of the Geological Survey for some years.
How many?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Probably four or five years. At the time of the death of Dr. Dawson his salary as geologist was $2,400. Dr. Bell was never made director of the survey for reasons that I am not aware of. I would suppose that the minister of that day did not think Dr. Bell possessed the strength and abilities which would fit him to be the permanent director of the survey. At all events, he was not appointed. He was acting director and he received, during that time, the salary of his position as geologist of the survey, $2,400. While he was acting director he declined, I understand, to accept the annual increase of salary appertaining to the position of geologist, claiming, I am advised, that during that time he should receive the
salary of director-. The minister did not see fit to accede to that claim. Mr. Low was appointed director, probably three years ago, Dr. Bell being at that time advanced to the position of chief geologist, a name created especially for the purpose of giving him a distinctive position in the .survey.
Did that carry an in-ei'ease of salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That carried an increase of salary up to $3,000. Dr. Bell has received $3,000 practically for three years, and on the 1st of June last he accepted superannuation, being given six months' leave of absence. He receives a superannuation allowance of a little over $2,000 a year. I am aware of the fact that Dr. Bell does claim the difference between the $2,400 per annum that he received as acting director and the present salary of director.
Which is?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: $3,000. Mr. Low, who occupies the position of director*, is also the head of the department, and his salary has been going up since by annual increases of, I think, $100. Dr. Bell, in my opinion, has been very fairly dealt with. He is receiving a superannuation allowance of over $2,000. He was not, in the opinion of the ministers who have administered the department for the last ten years, just the person that -they would cate to put into the position of director tor reasons I do not need to go into. He is an old official of the department ; I believe he has been over fifty years in the service. I do not believe it is accurate for the hon. gentleman to say that the whole or any portion of the work in the way of the publication of reports or surveys since Dr. Bell has retired from the service is due to the work of Dr. Bell further than that, of course, the surveys made by the Geological Survey during his administration annually have been published as the reports of the department. The principal part of the work done by the Mines Department during the last few years has been conceived and carried out by Dr. Low, the Director of the Geological Survey, and by Dr. Haanel, Director of the Mines branch. I understand that Dr. Bell does make some claim for compensation for the five years during which he has been acting director. That matter was presented to me a few weeks ago, and it has not been disposed of.

I was taking Jhe statement that the minister has made last. A geologist is a technical officer, and Dr. Bell has gvien some fifty years' service to Canada. When that fifty years was pretty well up to its limit, he was getting only $2,400 a year. Dr. Bell is a geologist of note, and it

does seem to me that there is every ground for treating him as an old scientific man, and one who has been, so long in the service, a little better than to keep him down to $2,100 when he was doing the work of director as well as it would have been done if he had been appointed director. The fact that he did not receive any annual increment for five or six years is also a consideration that weighs. Then you made him chief geologist at the very modest salary of $3,000. Within the last two weeks you have made salaries of $4,000 and $5,000 for gentlemen who have not spent fifty years in the service of the country, and are not scientific men or technical in any sense. It does seem to me that the minister has a very good reason for giving to Dr. Bell the difference between his salary and what would have been the salary of the director if there had been one during the period referred to. The minister says Dr. Bell gets a superannuation of $2,000 ; but why does he get it ? Because lie has given fifty years of service, not because of the very large salary on which he was retired. If a man has given fifty years of service, it is hardly right to cast into his teeth the fact that he gets $2,000 now, when lie has earned that superannuation on a very modest salary. I cannot help saying that other cases, and many of them, men without his abilities have been treated much more liberally. I think the minister would be doing a wise thing if he would make the proper readjustment in this case.

I would not be inclined to take the view which seems to have impressed Itself on the Minister of Mines with regard to Dr. Bell. If Dr. Bell was not competent to discharge the duties of director, those duties should not have been imposed upon him for a period of five years. I do not understand from the statement of the minister that there is any difference between the duties of a director and the duties of an acting director. For five years those duties were imposed on Dr. Bell, and during that time he did not receive the salary which ordinarily pertains to that office. Tlie Minister of the Interior was unfair either to the country or to Dr. Bell. If Dr. Bell was not competent to fill that position he should not have been invested with the duties of that office for five years, or for five months. On the other hand, if Dr. Bell was competent to discharge the duties of the office for five years, I see no reason why he should have been asked to do that without the salary he would have received if he had been formally appointed director. I was not impressed with the argument of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I made no argument. I simply stated facts.

The hon. gentleman stated that Dr. Bell had been very Mr. FOSTER.
fairly treated, giving as a reason that his salary had been increased for the last three years of his service. Suppose his salary had been increased for ten years to $3,000, that argument would fall to the ground, and Dr. Bell would have been in a much better position. I have the impression, from a debate which took place in the committee of supply two or three years ago, that on a previous occasion a gentleman had been allowed the salary of director during the period in which he fulfilled as acting director the duties of the office. That is a precedent which it seems to me should not be departed from without very good reason. I do trust that the minister will take this matter into consideration, and give to Dr. Bell, who is a scientist of great repute, the treatment which I think the country can well afford to him after fifty years of faithful service.

I hold in my hand a computation of the amount of difference between the salary which Dr. Bell drew as acting director and the salary that would have been paid to a director for the five years from the 1st of March, 1901, when he was appointed acting director. The difference amounts to $4,591. I agree with what has been said as to the advisability of doing something for Dr. Bell, who has been in the service for so lo-ng a time. It appears to me that the minister has a precedent for remunerating Dr. Bell for the services rendered by him, in the case of Dr. Dawson, who was paid an extra $1,000 as acting director for one year in 1896, when Dr. Sel-wyn was absent in Europe. 1 hope the minister will see his way to consider favourably the suggestion to remunerate Dr. Bell for the time he acted as director.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
With regard to Dr. Dawson, he was one of the most eminent scientists Canada ever produced and one of the most successful directors of our geological survey. I do not understand that it is customary, where an official acts for another \ in a superior position, as, for instance, where a chief clerk acts for a deputy minister, to pay him the salary of the superior officer.
My knowledge of the salaries of acting deputy ministers is very limited, and I speak subject to correction. I agree with the remarks made by the hon. member for North Toronto in regard to the inadequacy of the salaries not only of the acting director of that day and of the acting director of this day, but of the officers of the Geologicai Survey generally. We have men in the survey who have been twenty or twenty-five years in the service and who are receiving now less than $2,000. I do not think that is creditable. I hope that, under the reorganization of the department, the technical men will get a certain standing and advance more rapidly than in the past and the whole department be put on a better footing in this respect. With regard to Dr.

Bell, I have very little to say. While he was acting director he received his old salary. He refused to accept the annual increment of $50 or $100 whichever it was,.because as he then claimed, and has since claimed, he should receive the salary applicable to the position. No doubt he is fairly entitled to the annual increment. Whether he should or should not receive the salary belonging to the office at the time I am not prepared to say. We have had an acting director, Mr. Brook, for the last year who is receiving only $2,300.
He has not been fifty years in the service.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No, but he has been ten or fifteen years in the service. But that does not effect the principle. He has been receiving for the last year, not the salary of the director, but the salary he was receiving before as geologist of the department, $2,300. I put a sum in the estimate to bring his salary up to $2,800 because he is a capable acting director. I am sorry to say that Mr. Low is not in a position to return to the department. He is director and deputy head and is receiving the salary of the position. But he is now away on sick leave. He is not entitled to superannuation; he is a very superior man and most efficient director, and we hope he will return to his duties soon. But Mr. Brock is not receiving $3,000 but is being treated the same as Dr. Bell. As long as Mr. Low is away Mr. Brock will receive simply the salary paid him as geologist of the department, which this year, will be $2,800. In making the change from Dr. Bell to another, who is permanent director, I believe that the interest of the public service has been promoted.

I do not wish to be understood as suggesting that when a chief clerk, in the case of the temporary absence or license of the deputy head, performs the duty of that office for a short time, he necessarily should be paid the salary of the office for that period. But the case to which I have alluded was not a case of that kind. The office had become vacant and for a period of five years an official of the department was charged with the duties of the office. It seems to me that a case of that kind stands upon an entirely different plane and that some consideration at least should be given to the fact that for so long a time and under such circumstances he did perform the duties of the office to the best of his ability, and the country received the benefit of his services in that capacity.
Dominion of Canada assay office-maintenance of assay office, Vancouver, British Colombia, $13,500.
I would like to have some information from the minister as to what is being done in the assay office in Vancouver -as to the results, say, for the past year.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I regret to say that I have not read the report of last year. But I was advised by the Director of Mines branch, Dr. Haanel, that the receipts of gold at Vancouver assay office during the last two months had been far in excess of any previous term of similar length. The receipts for the six months were about $4,000,-OOO. Extra help was required for the handling of the gold. I am glad to say that the utility of the assay office has been demonstrated more clearly than ever.
Geological Survey branch-explorations and surveys; printing and publishing reports, maps, &c.; wages of assistant explorers, draughtsmen, clerks and others; purchase of specimens, (books, instruments, stationery, mapping materials, maintenance of offices and museum, laboratory apparatus, chemicals, miscellaneous expenses, &c., $45,000.

I desire to say just a word as to what appears to me to be the questionable plan of having the officers of the Geological Survey branch, sometimes in the department and sometimes out of it. From information we have bad, it seems that these officers, when out of the department, take part in what might be called private explorations, that is, exploration work for private parties or corporations, being used in such a way that it is quite possible the private parties or corporations may avail themselves of the special knowledge the officer has gained while under pay of the Dominion and be greatly profited thereby- I do not mean by his generak'knowledge as geologist or expert of any kind, hut by his knowledge of the richness of localities. Does the minister think it good policy to have these officers for a time in the department, then working for private corporations, then back again doing exploration work for the Dominion ? I understand that one of the officers of the department is going across the water, we paying his salary and expenses, though the work he will do is absolutely in the interest of a speculative company. I think that refers to a company in New Brunswick, in which Mr. Lodge of whom we have heard in the House, is interested. I think this is making a very different use of the officers of the department from what one would think correct. I understand that quite a number of officers in the hon. gentleman's department are like the revolving lights, at one time flashing in the department, then obscured to the department and flashing somewhere else, then returning to light up the department again.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The point raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) is a very important one. There is a good deal to he said on both sides of that question. The hon. member speaks as though many of the officials were appearing in and disappearing from the survey to do work for private parties. I think there are very few instances of that kind on record alto-

gether. This year there have been only two so far as my recollection serves. With reference to sending Dr. Ells to Glasgow to watch the process of the extraction of oil from the shales of New Brunswick, that is wholly in the interest of the public. It is not in the interest of the company or the individual, it is entirely in the interest of the Geological Survey. He has knowledge of the existence of shales and their extent and knows something of the probability of oil extraction therefrom, but he will acquire information as to the extraction by watching the operation, will make a report to the Geological Survey and that report will be published in the interest of the people of the country. It is not in the interest of the New Brunswick company, except iu a general way, through the information that will be made public. I think in that respect it was perfectly proper and fair to pay his expenses which I was informed would not be more than $500.

This shale is being cruushed in the old country, and the object is to find out how much oil it will produce and if it is economical and commercially valuable in that way. You send Dr. Ells, as a member of the Geological Survey, to watch the operation and make up his mind as to what value there is in those shales. Does that seem to be the object of the formation of the Geological Survey ? Would their duty not be more to locate generally the existence and extent of these shales ? This would seem to be rather a malversation.
Mr. ' TEMPLEMAN. There are two branches of the Department of Mines, the Geological Survey, which is technical and scientific, and the Mines branch, which is practical and economic. Dr. Ells is an economic geologist, but he was sent to Scotland by Dr. Haanel, of the Mines Branch, to obtain information of importance in respect to these shales. This is absolutely along the lines of our action in regard to the peat deposits of Ontario. We sent a member of the Mines Branch to Europe last year and he has published a very valuable and useful report on the peat deposits and the manufacture of peat into fuel in Europe. At the time of the discovery of the nickel deposits at Sudbury the department pursued the same policy, and the report of the official then sent there was of great value in the inauguration of the mining industry at Sudbury. It must be remembered that one of the great difficulties we have in connection with the work of the Geological Survey is the scarcity in Canada of men qualified for the work of the department.

I want to emphasize what I said this afternoon, that I do not see anything in the past practice of this parliament which authorizes increases in special salaries out of a general vote or what may be left over from a general vote. No department, because it has a general vote which it has not used up, can out of that vote go behind parliament and raise the salaries of a dozen or twenty clerks. The universal practice has been that before you can raise the salary of a clerk whose salary (has been voted by this parliament, you must come to parliament and get the money for doing that; and I do not see how it is possible, in the case of the House of Commons any more than in the case of a department, to raise the salaries of a number of clerks without parliamentary authority,
and to raise them from a period which antedates the time of the action. I am not saying this because I want to bar the increases to the officers of the House, but I am expressing a principle which I think is absolutely clear and definite, and I would be very sorry to see the House of Commons itself break one of the fundamental rules of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There seems to be some question as to the proper procedure in the matter. I am not sure that this is without precedent, though I am not sure that it is a wise practice to pay such increases out of general votes. I have not had the point brought before me before, and I will look into it. There is no desire to depart from sound rules in the matter.

I do not think there is, and I mention it in the same spirit in which the Finance Minister refers to it. I would be very sorry, if there were.
Department of Finance and Treasury Board- To provide for the appointment of .T. G. Artz as second-class clerk at a salary of $1,350 per annum, $900.	,
Might I be allowed to call the attention of the Finance Minister to this ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Artz is a gentleman whose services we could not obtain without this vote. He is a chartered accountant, a gentleman of considerable experience, the sort of man likely to be useful in the department, and we have had to take this special vote to give him an adequate salary. He has passed the civil service examination.
Is this gentleman to be the actuary?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, I contemplate making Mr. Grant the actuary. As a chartered accountant and a man of considerable experience, Mr. Artz could not be expected to enter the service at the ordinary salary, and we have had to fix his salary at this rate, which is a very moderate rate, to secure his services.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Bill has been prepared by the clerks in the usual form.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the House that a message has been received from the Senate sending certain amendments to Bill (No. 115) to amend the Dominion Elections Act, to which they ask the concurrence of this House.
Amendments read the first time.
What are the amendments ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The only amendment made to this Bill appeal's to be in the Mr. MACDONALD.
provision as to the date when the county judges in Manitoba shall be called together to appoint committees of their number. The provision in the Bill as it left this House was that the several judges of the county court should constitute a board, and that that board should during the month of July in each year meet in the city of Winnipeg on a day to be named. The amendment consists in substituting for the words 'during the month of July' the words 'between the 1st of July and the 15th day of August ' ; that is extending for two weeks the period during which the judges may meet. It does not occur to me that there is anything in the amendment to which objection should he taken, and I beg to move concurrence.
Amendments read the second time and agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thought we might have completed our business and arranged to meet on Monday at 11.45 with a view to have prorogation at noon. As there are several Bills to come from the Senate, we had better meet at the usual hour. I beg to move that ithe House do now adjourn.
